domain.name: System Design
domain.description: Learn the building blocks, then work through systems and company cases across 18 chapters and 200 learning units.

domainCoverage.synopsis: Learn the building blocks, then work through systems and company cases across 18 chapters and 200 learning units.

chapters.title: Quorum Consistency & Raft Consensus
chapters.summary: Data replication copies datasets across multiple network nodes to ensure high availability, read scalability, and disaster fault tolerance. Managing replicas forces architects to navigate the fundamental trade-off between strong consistency (immediate linearizability) and high availability during network partitions (CAP and PACELC Theorems).

chapters.title: Message Queues & DLQ Backpressure
chapters.summary: Message queues decouple producers from consumers, holding job tasks in RAM/disk until worker pools process them.

chapters.title: Event-Driven Architecture & Message Streaming
chapters.summary: Event-driven architecture replaces synchronous REST HTTP calls with asynchronous event publishing (Kafka/RabbitMQ), ensuring high throughput and fault isolation.

modules.title: Fundamentals: Foundations
modules.description: Clarify requirements, estimate capacity, and decide which complexity the system needs.

concepts.title: Requirements clarification
concepts.summary: Techniques for uncovering ambiguous business expectations, functional limits, and core system constraints.

concepts.title: Logical system design
concepts.summary: Translating product workflows into logical components, data boundaries, and clean entity relationships.

concepts.title: Non-functional requirements
concepts.summary: Defining precise latency SLAs, availability targets (nines), durability requirements, and throughput goals.

concepts.title: System design tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Evaluating architectural compromises: read vs write optimization, simplicity vs flexibility, and speed vs cost.

concepts.title: Availability, durability, consistency, cost
concepts.summary: The four fundamental axes of system trade-offs and how they dictate technology choices.

concepts.title: Back-of-the-envelope capacity planning
concepts.summary: Calculating QPS, peak multipliers, network bandwidth, storage growth over 5 years, and memory working sets.

concepts.title: How a server handles many requests
concepts.summary: Process models, multi-threading, asynchronous I/O event loops (epoll/kqueue), and thread pool saturation.

concepts.title: Horizontal vs vertical scaling
concepts.summary: Evaluating vertical headroom (CPUs, NVMe, RAM) against horizontal stateless clustering and data partitioning.

concepts.title: Monolith vs microservices
concepts.summary: Architectural decision boundaries: team autonomy, independent deployment cycles, and RPC overhead.

concepts.title: Repository pattern
concepts.summary: Decoupling domain business logic from data access layers to enable safe storage migration and mocking.

concepts.title: Extensible data modeling
concepts.summary: Designing schema entities that support schema evolution, polymorphism, and backward compatibility.

concepts.title: Cost-aware architecture
concepts.summary: Optimizing compute instances, data transfer egress fees, tiered storage, and reserved capacity economics.

concepts.title: When not to add infrastructure
concepts.summary: The operational burden of distributed components and how to push existing infrastructure to its physical limits.

theory.overview: Every large-scale architecture begins with defining functional scope, clarifying non-functional constraints (latency, throughput, durability, availability), and calculating back-of-the-envelope capacity bounds. Premature distributed infrastructure introduces catastrophic operational complexity; senior architects evaluate the trade-offs between vertical scaling, monolithic boundaries, and distributed microservices before introducing network hops.
theory.whyItMatters: Failing to establish clear non-functional targets leads to mismatched storage engines, runaway cloud bills, and unmaintainable architectures. Estimating QPS and data growth upfront determines whether a single PostgreSQL instance suffices or whether sharded distributed storage is mathematically required.
keyMechanisms: Back-of-the-envelope estimation: translating DAU, read/write ratios, and retention into QPS, network bandwidth, and disk IOPS.
Availability vs Durability vs Consistency: balancing SLAs (99.99%) against RPO (Recovery Point Objective) and RTO (Recovery Time Objective).
Monolith vs Microservices: Conway's law, deployment boundaries, and the operational cost of RPC failure domains.
Extensible data modeling: repository isolation and domain-driven design preventing database lock-in.

modules.title: Fundamentals: APIs, Services and Protocols
modules.description: Choose service boundaries and communication patterns, then handle retries and overload.

concepts.title: API design contracts
concepts.summary: Crafting robust REST, GraphQL, and RPC contracts with explicit versioning and backward compatibility.

concepts.title: Service-to-service communication
concepts.summary: Evaluating synchronous RPC vs asynchronous messaging and choreography vs orchestration.

concepts.title: HTTP, REST, and gRPC
concepts.summary: Protobuf serialization, HTTP/2 multiplexing, binary framing, and streaming RPC trade-offs.

concepts.title: TCP vs UDP
concepts.summary: Connection-oriented reliable delivery vs connectionless low-latency packet streaming (QUIC / HTTP/3).

concepts.title: API gateway vs load balancer
concepts.summary: Reverse proxy routing, SSL termination, request authentication, rate limiting, and edge aggregation.

concepts.title: Load balancers
concepts.summary: Round-robin, least connections, weighted routing, health checking, and high-availability VRRP/BGP pairs.

concepts.title: Consistent-hashing load balancing
concepts.summary: Minimizing cache remapping during server addition/removal using virtual ring slots and bounded loads.

concepts.title: Event contracts
concepts.summary: Schema registries (Avro, Protobuf), event versioning, forward/backward compatibility, and payload evolution.

concepts.title: Retries, timeouts, and idempotency
concepts.summary: Configuring deadlines, exponential backoff with full jitter, and deterministic idempotency token tracking.

concepts.title: Batching
concepts.summary: Amortizing network and database round-trips by grouping requests into micro-batches with bounded wait times.

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.summary: Propagating downstream consumer saturation upstream to prevent out-of-memory crashes and thread exhaustion.

concepts.title: Tail latency
concepts.summary: Mitigating p99 latency spikes via hedged requests, speculative retries, and tied-deadline task cancellation.

concepts.title: Load shedding
concepts.summary: Dropping low-priority traffic (background jobs, non-critical telemetry) when CPU or queue delay exceeds SLAs.

theory.overview: Service interaction patterns define system coupling and latency characteristics. Architects choose between synchronous RPC (REST, gRPC) and asynchronous message events, configure layer-4 and layer-7 load balancing, and install overload defenses such as backpressure, token-bucket rate limiting, tail latency mitigation, and priority load shedding.
theory.whyItMatters: Synchronous network calls propagate latency tail percentiles and cascade downstream outages. Without explicit timeouts, circuit breakers, and idempotency guarantees, client retry loops trigger self-inflicted denial-of-service retry storms.
keyMechanisms: Transport layer protocols: TCP connection handshakes, congestion control, head-of-line blocking, and UDP / QUIC benefits.
L4 vs L7 load balancing: TCP proxying vs HTTP path routing, SSL termination, and consistent hashing.
Retry resilience: exponential backoff with full jitter and idempotency key caching to eliminate duplicate side effects.
Overload control: token bucket rate limiting, queue-based backpressure, tail latency hedging, and load shedding.

modules.title: Fundamentals: Data Modeling and SQL
modules.description: Study data modeling, indexing, query planning, and relational scaling.

concepts.title: Relational database design
concepts.summary: Normal forms, entity relationships, referential integrity, and intentional denormalization for read efficiency.

concepts.title: Design: a key-value store on SQL
concepts.summary: Implementing high-throughput key-value lookups over SQL tables using optimized clustered primary keys.

concepts.title: Database indexing
concepts.summary: Clustered vs non-clustered indexes, covering indexes, selectivity, and composite index column ordering rules.

concepts.title: B-tree
concepts.summary: Physical disk page layout, node splitting, tree rebalancing, fanout, and cache-friendly leaf traversal.

concepts.title: Query planning
concepts.summary: EXPLAIN execution plans, index scans vs sequential scans, cost-based optimization, and join algorithms (hash vs merge).

concepts.title: Database locking and isolation
concepts.summary: Shared and exclusive locks, two-phase locking (2PL), deadlock detection, and ANSI isolation levels.

concepts.title: MVCC
concepts.summary: Multi-Version Concurrency Control, snapshot isolation, tuple visibility rules, and dead tuple vacuuming overhead.

concepts.title: Database WAL and recovery
concepts.summary: Write-ahead logging, fsync durability, checkpointing, and crash recovery via ARIES redo/undo protocols.

concepts.title: Database ticket servers
concepts.summary: Centralized sequence generators (Flickr ticket servers) vs auto-increment offsets for unique primary keys.

concepts.title: Relational database scaling
concepts.summary: Read replicas, asynchronous replication lag, connection pooling (PgBouncer), and vertical scaling limits.

concepts.title: Online indexing
concepts.summary: Building secondary indexes concurrently on production tables without blocking mutating DML queries.

concepts.title: Schema evolution
concepts.summary: Zero-downtime database migrations: expand-and-contract pattern, shadow tables, and backward-compatible DDL.

concepts.title: Soft delete
concepts.summary: Handling logical deletion with deleted_at timestamps, partial indexes, and archival strategies for fast scans.

theory.overview: Relational databases form the bedrock of transactional consistency. Mastering B-Tree physical layouts, query optimizer execution plans, ACID isolation anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, write skew), and Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) enables engineers to scale SQL databases through read replication, online indexing, and non-blocking schema evolution.
theory.whyItMatters: Suboptimal indexes and unconstrained transactions result in table locks, query timeouts, and database replication lag. Understanding write-ahead logs (WAL) and MVCC mechanics is necessary to prevent production outages during large-scale data migrations and schema alterations.
keyMechanisms: B-Tree indexing: page fills, clustered vs secondary indexes, index selectivity, and composite index ordering.
ACID isolation levels: Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable implemented via two-phase locking or SSI.
MVCC & WAL recovery: append-only durability logs, undo/redo buffers, vacuuming dead tuples, and crash recovery.
Online operations: ghost tables, shadow columns, dual-writing, and soft-delete index optimizations.

modules.title: Fundamentals: NoSQL, Partitioning and IDs
modules.description: Study NoSQL decision boundaries, partitioning, sharding, and distributed ID generation.

concepts.title: NoSQL decision boundaries
concepts.summary: When to abandon relational ACID for horizontal scalability, schemaless documents, or high-write wide-column models.

concepts.title: Document vs key-value stores
concepts.summary: JSON document nested querying (MongoDB) vs ultra-fast O(1) point lookups by key (Redis, DynamoDB).

concepts.title: Columnar vs wide-column stores
concepts.summary: OLAP columnar storage (ClickHouse/Parquet) vs Bigtable/Cassandra sparse multi-dimensional sorted maps.

concepts.title: Graph database decision boundary
concepts.summary: Property graphs, index-free adjacency, and traversal queries (Neo4j) vs relational recursive CTEs.

concepts.title: Sharding and partitioning
concepts.summary: Partitioning data horizontally across distinct database servers using partition keys and routing tiers.

concepts.title: Hot partitions
concepts.summary: Identifying and mitigating uneven traffic distribution, celebrity keys, and write bottleneck skew.

concepts.title: Consistent hashing
concepts.summary: Virtual node mapping across a 2^32 ring to ensure minimal key migration when scaling nodes up or down.

concepts.title: Distributed ID generation
concepts.summary: Generating globally unique 64-bit identifiers across hundreds of nodes without centralized database locks.

concepts.title: UUID, ObjectId, and Snowflake
concepts.summary: Evaluating UUIDv4 randomness and index fragmentation against time-ordered ObjectId and 64-bit Snowflake IDs.

concepts.title: Snowflake ID design
concepts.summary: Bit allocation: 41-bit millisecond epoch, 10-bit machine/datacenter ID, and 12-bit sequence counter mechanics.

concepts.title: Clock skew and ID ordering
concepts.summary: NTP synchronization drift, backward clock jumps, and leasing safety mechanisms in ID generation.

concepts.title: Keyset pagination
concepts.summary: Eliminating slow OFFSET/LIMIT database pagination using cursor-based where id > last_seen order by id limit N.

concepts.title: Bloom filters
concepts.summary: Space-efficient probabilistic bitsets used to skip costly disk reads for non-existent partition keys.

concepts.title: Hot and cold storage, archival
concepts.summary: Tiering data lifecycles from fast NVMe storage to low-cost S3 Glacier cold object storage.

theory.overview: When data scale exceeds single-server storage limits, systems partition data across horizontal nodes. This module covers document, key-value, wide-column, and graph storage boundaries; range-based vs hash-based partitioning; mitigating hot partition hotspots; consistent hashing rings; and 64-bit distributed unique ID generation (Snowflake, UUIDv7).
theory.whyItMatters: Poor partition key selection causes skewed partitions where a single node handles 90% of traffic, crashing the cluster. Distributed primary keys must be time-sortable to ensure efficient B-tree index locality without requiring coordinated centralized locking.
keyMechanisms: NoSQL taxonomies: document (JSON), wide-column (SSTable/Cassandra), key-value, and graph database trade-offs.
Sharding strategies: hash partitioning vs range partitioning, directory lookup tables, and resharding rebalances.
Hot partitions: salt keys, synthetic split keys, and read-side caching to mitigate partition skew.
Distributed ID generation: Twitter Snowflake timestamp + machine ID + sequence structure ensuring k-ordered uniqueness.

modules.title: Fundamentals: Caching and Fast Reads
modules.description: Place caches, keep their contents useful, and plan for misses and failures.

concepts.title: Caching layers
concepts.summary: Browser caches, CDN edge proxies, API gateway caches, Redis in-memory tiers, and local process heap caches.

concepts.title: Distributed cache design
concepts.summary: Clustering Redis/Memcached instances with client-side hashing, master-replica replication, and memory limits.

concepts.title: Cache eviction policies
concepts.summary: Comparing LRU, LFU, FIFO, and ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) for different workload access patterns.

concepts.title: TTL expiration and cache reapers
concepts.summary: Active vs passive TTL expiration, background sweeper threads, and adding jitter to avoid synchronized expiration.

concepts.title: Cache concurrency control
concepts.summary: Preventing dogpiling, thundering herds, and cache stampedes using distributed mutexes and singleflight locks.

concepts.title: Cache availability and database fallback
concepts.summary: Circuit breakers, graceful degraded read modes, and protecting the primary database when the cache tier drops.

theory.overview: Caching intercepts reads to eliminate slow disk and database queries. Designing robust cache tiers requires choosing between cache-aside, write-through, and write-behind patterns; configuring eviction policies (LRU, LFU, 2Q); managing TTL jitter to prevent cache stampedes; and engineering fallback paths when cache clusters fail.
theory.whyItMatters: A cache miss rate increasing from 1% to 10% can ten-fold downstream database load, causing immediate database collapse. Systems must withstand thundering herds and dogpiling when hot keys expire.
keyMechanisms: Cache topologies: in-memory process caches vs distributed Redis clusters and multi-tier edge CDN caching.
Eviction algorithms: Least Recently Used (doubly linked list + hash map), LFU, and sliding TTL reapers.
Stampede mitigation: probabilistic early expiration (XFetch), mutex locking on cache miss, and background warmers.
Cache invalidation consistency: dual-write hazards, CDC-based invalidation, and TTL boundaries.

modules.title: Fundamentals: Distributed Coordination
modules.description: Reason about replication, agreement, locks, clocks, and consistency.

concepts.title: Distributed systems foundations
concepts.summary: Unreliable networks, partial failure modes, crash-stop vs crash-recovery, and asynchronous network assumptions.

concepts.title: Consistency models
concepts.summary: Linearizability, sequential consistency, causal consistency, read-your-writes, and eventual convergence.

concepts.title: Replication
concepts.summary: Single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication, sync vs async durability trade-offs.

concepts.title: CAP and PACELC
concepts.summary: Formal proof of partition trade-offs and latency vs consistency trade-offs during normal cluster operation.

concepts.title: Clocks and ordering
concepts.summary: Physical clock drift, NTP synchronization limits, Lamport logical clocks, and causality-tracking Vector clocks.

concepts.title: Consensus
concepts.summary: The consensus problem, FLP impossibility result, and majority quorum agreement mechanics.

concepts.title: Leader election
concepts.summary: Raft election timeouts, split vote avoidance, and term numbers preventing dual-leader split brain.

concepts.title: Distributed locks and leases
concepts.summary: Time-bounded leases, lease renewal heartbeats, and why wall-clock timeouts cannot guarantee exclusive locks.

concepts.title: Redis Redlock and fencing tokens
concepts.summary: Analyzing Redlock failure scenarios under network pauses and using monotonically increasing fencing tokens.

concepts.title: Circuit breakers and timeouts
concepts.summary: State machines (Closed, Open, Half-Open) tripping on error thresholds to isolate failing distributed peers.

concepts.title: Gossip protocol
concepts.summary: Epidemic dissemination, decentralized cluster membership, failure detection, and SWIM protocol mechanics.

concepts.title: Metadata service and node discovery
concepts.summary: Using consistent coordination stores (etcd, Consul) for dynamic service registry and configuration delivery.

concepts.title: Distributed hash tables
concepts.summary: P2P decentralized routing, Kademlia XOR metric, routing tables, and logarithmic hop lookups.

theory.overview: Coordinating state across independent physical machines without shared memory is the central challenge of distributed systems. This module covers consensus protocols (Raft, Paxos), leader election, distributed locking and fencing tokens, gossip-based membership discovery, clock synchronization (Lamport, Vector, TrueTime), and the CAP/PACELC theorem.
theory.whyItMatters: Uncoordinated distributed writes cause split-brain data divergence, where two nodes accept conflicting updates simultaneously. Without monotonically increasing fencing tokens, delayed packets or garbage-collection pauses allow zombie leaders to corrupt state.
keyMechanisms: Consensus & Quorums: Raft state machine replication, leader heartbeats, term elections, and write quorums.
Distributed locking: Redis Redlock pitfalls, ZooKeeper / etcd ephemeral sequential znodes, and generation fencing.
Ordering without wall-clocks: Lamport logical clocks, vector causality tracking, and hybrid logical clocks (HLC).
Node discovery: gossip protocols (SWIM), heartbeating, failure detectors, and distributed hash tables (Kademlia).

modules.title: Fundamentals: Storage Engines
modules.description: Follow how databases and object stores organize, persist, and retrieve bytes.

concepts.title: Storage engine design constraints
concepts.summary: Physical disk characteristics: sequential NVMe throughput vs random 4KB read seeks and write endurance.

concepts.title: Storage engine tradeoffs
concepts.summary: The RUM Conjecture: balancing Read overhead, Update cost, and Memory/storage footprint.

concepts.title: A file-backed dictionary
concepts.summary: Building a rudimentary file-backed key-value store using append-only logs and in-memory byte offsets.

concepts.title: Custom binary file format
concepts.summary: Designing binary packet formats with magic bytes, field length headers, CRC32 checksums, and alignment.

concepts.title: Byte-range indexed object storage
concepts.summary: Retrieving arbitrary file slices efficiently using HTTP Range headers and index offset lookup maps.

concepts.title: Immutable versioned data files
concepts.summary: Why immutable files eliminate locking bugs and simplify multi-version concurrent reading.

concepts.title: Log-structured storage
concepts.summary: Append-only logs as the universal abstraction for crash recovery, replication streams, and high write ingestion.

concepts.title: Bitcask storage engine
concepts.summary: Log-structured key-value engine with an all-RAM hash index (keydir) and append-only disk segments.

concepts.title: LSM-tree storage engine
concepts.summary: Log-Structured Merge-Tree foundations: optimizing for high-throughput writes by deferring and batching disk writes.

concepts.title: Memtable, WAL, and SSTable
concepts.summary: In-memory sorted buffer (Memtable), durable write-ahead log (WAL), and flushed sorted disk files (SSTable).

concepts.title: LSM read path: Bloom filters and sparse index
concepts.summary: Pruning disk seeks on SSTables using sparse primary key indexes and probabilistic Bloom filters.

concepts.title: Compaction and amplification
concepts.summary: Size-tiered vs leveled compaction, tombstone deletions, and minimizing write/space amplification.

concepts.title: Object storage vs database
concepts.summary: Key architectural boundaries: blob immutability, flat metadata hierarchies, and cost per gigabyte.

concepts.title: S3 object storage architecture
concepts.summary: Internal architecture of hyperscale object storage: request routers, partition map tables, and storage nodes.

concepts.title: Range partitioning vs consistent hashing for storage
concepts.summary: Trade-offs between range-based partitioning (efficient prefix scanning) and hash rings (even distribution).

concepts.title: Partition manager and map table
concepts.summary: Centralized and distributed partition managers tracking ownership of billions of storage blocks.

concepts.title: Metadata database for object storage
concepts.summary: Separating high-IOPS metadata (permissions, tags, versions) from raw immutable payload byte storage.

concepts.title: Append-only stream layer
concepts.summary: Building durable commit log services that underpin storage replication and event distribution.

concepts.title: Durability and replication
concepts.summary: Reed-Solomon erasure coding vs 3x cross-datacenter replication for eleven nines of durability at minimal cost.

concepts.title: End-to-end checksums
concepts.summary: Detecting silent bit-rot and network transport corruption using end-to-end SHA-256 and CRC32 checks.

theory.overview: Storage engines determine how data is laid out on physical NVMe/SSD disks and retrieved in memory. This comprehensive module covers log-structured append-only storage, Bitcask key-value engines, Log-Structured Merge-Trees (LSM-trees with Memtables, WALs, and SSTables), write/read/space amplification, and cloud object store (S3) architectures including partition maps and chunked byte-range indexing.
theory.whyItMatters: Databases spend 90% of their CPU and I/O on storage engine compaction and page indexing. Understanding LSM-tree compaction stalls and write amplification allows architects to pick the right engine for write-heavy vs read-heavy production workloads.
keyMechanisms: Append-only persistence: sequential disk I/O vs random seeks, immutable segments, and write-ahead logging.
LSM-Tree architecture: in-memory skiplist Memtables, append-only WAL, immutable SSTables, and Bloom filter pruning.
Compaction strategies: size-tiered vs leveled compaction, managing write amplification and disk I/O spikes.
Object storage internals: chunking, content-addressable storage, range indexing, and partition map management.

modules.title: Fundamentals: Async Work and Streams
modules.description: Separate background work from requests and handle retries, ordering, and contention.

concepts.title: Delegation and async work
concepts.summary: Decoupling user response latency from asynchronous background tasks via durable message handoff.

concepts.title: Task queue vs event stream
concepts.summary: Point-to-point task queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) vs append-only partition-ordered event streams (Kafka).

concepts.title: Event bus for product events
concepts.summary: Publish-subscribe messaging decoupling domain services through asynchronous broadcast events.

concepts.title: Queue lag
concepts.summary: Monitoring consumer lag metrics, partition offsets, and processing throughput to scale worker pools.

concepts.title: Distributed task scheduler
concepts.summary: Building cron schedulers across clusters using distributed locking and leader-follower coordination.

concepts.title: Postgres SKIP LOCKED work queue
concepts.summary: High-throughput transactional queue processing directly in SQL without deadlocks or row contention.

concepts.title: DAG workflow orchestration
concepts.summary: Orchestrating multi-step asynchronous directed acyclic graphs with retry policies and compensation sagas.

concepts.title: Rule engine and trigger framework
concepts.summary: Event-driven condition evaluation, action dispatching, and rate-limited trigger pipelines.

concepts.title: Fanout patterns
concepts.summary: Worker pool fanout, chunked topic partitioning, and dead letter queue routing for millions of recipients.

concepts.title: Flash sale inventory locking
concepts.summary: Handling extreme write contention on hot items using Redis atomic DECR, token reservation, and timeouts.

theory.overview: Separating synchronous request-response execution from heavyweight background tasks prevents thread exhaustion and buffers spikes in user traffic. This module covers message queues vs event logs, queue lag telemetry, distributed task scheduling, Postgres SKIP LOCKED work queues, DAG workflow orchestration, fanout patterns, and flash sale inventory reservation.
theory.whyItMatters: Synchronously executing image resizing, payment capture, or batch emails within HTTP handlers causes request timeouts and cascades worker thread exhaustion. Asynchronous workers must guarantee at-least-once processing without dropping jobs.
keyMechanisms: Queue vs Log models: RabbitMQ/SQS point-to-point competing consumers vs Kafka/Pulsar partition-ordered replayable logs.
Queue lag monitoring: alerting on consumer lag before buffer backlogs exceed memory limits.
Postgres SKIP LOCKED: implementing lightweight, ACID-compliant transactional work queues without Redis.
DAG orchestration: state machine workflow runners (Temporal, Airflow) handling compensation on failure.

modules.title: Fundamentals: Search and Retrieval
modules.description: Build indexes, process queries, and retrieve useful results.

concepts.title: Information retrieval system design
concepts.summary: High-level architecture of search systems: ingestion crawlers, tokenizers, indexing, and query evaluation.

concepts.title: Inverted index and posting lists
concepts.summary: Mapping terms to sorted document IDs, skip pointers, and delta-encoded compressed posting lists.

concepts.title: Boolean and tiered search

concepts.title: TF-IDF relevance scoring

concepts.title: BM25 production ranking
concepts.summary: Best Matching 25 ranking algorithm: handling term frequency saturation and document length normalization.

concepts.title: Stop words and champion lists
concepts.summary: Pruning high-frequency stop words and precomputing top-tier document candidate lists for speed.

concepts.title: Query understanding pipeline
concepts.summary: Spell correction, lemmatization, stemming, synonym expansion, and entity extraction on search inputs.

concepts.title: Search feedback and relevance signals
concepts.summary: Incorporating click-through rates (CTR), dwell time, and conversion signals into ranking algorithms.

concepts.title: Search evaluation metrics
concepts.summary: Measuring search quality using Precision@k, Recall@k, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and NDCG.

concepts.title: Search index synchronization
concepts.summary: Near real-time index synchronization from primary databases using CDC logs and change streams.

concepts.title: Search index sharding
concepts.summary: Partitioning large indexes across cluster nodes: document-based partitioning vs term-based partitioning.

concepts.title: Crawler and indexing pipeline
concepts.summary: Distributed web crawler architecture: politeness policies, robots.txt, deduplication, and link graph extractors.

concepts.title: Vector search and hybrid retrieval
concepts.summary: Dense vector embeddings, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN/HNSW), and reciprocal rank fusion with BM25.

concepts.title: Design: autocomplete
concepts.summary: Architecting low-latency prefix search with Tries, frequency caching, and client-side debouncing.

concepts.title: Design: did-you-mean and spell correction
concepts.summary: Levenshtein edit distance, n-gram phonetic matching, and noisy channel spelling correction.

concepts.title: Design: related searches

concepts.title: Design: recent searches
concepts.summary: Storing and evicting per-user recent search histories using Redis sorted sets and local device caches.

theory.overview: Search engines index unstructured text to answer fuzzy queries with sub-50ms latency. This deep module explores inverted indexes, posting lists, boolean and tiered scoring, TF-IDF and BM25 production ranking, query parsing pipelines, vector search (HNSW, ANN), search index sharding, and real-time typeahead autocomplete.
theory.whyItMatters: Relational LIKE queries scan millions of rows sequentially, crashing under load. Search engines require dedicated inverted indices and distributed sharding to rank millions of documents by semantic relevance within milliseconds.
keyMechanisms: Inverted index structures: dictionary term lexicons, compressed posting lists (Roaring Bitmaps), and term offsets.
Relevance scoring: BM25 term frequency saturation, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization.
Vector embeddings: dense vector similarity (cosine, dot product) combined with keyword BM25 in hybrid search.
Typeahead autocomplete: Trie memory structures, prefix trees, and precomputed candidate lists with caching.

modules.title: Fundamentals: Analytics and Sketches

concepts.title: Counting at scale

concepts.title: View counting at scale

concepts.title: Impression counting

concepts.title: HyperLogLog cardinality estimation
concepts.summary: Estimating billions of unique elements with 1.5 KB memory using hashing and leading-zero register tracking.

concepts.title: Mergeable sketches for analytics
concepts.summary: Combining partial sketch registers from distributed worker nodes via commutative and associative union operations.

concepts.title: Bucketed time-window aggregation
concepts.summary: Tumbling and sliding time windows aggregating event metrics into fixed-interval minute/hour buckets.

concepts.title: Raw events vs derived analytics
concepts.summary: Lambda and Kappa architectures: streaming real-time fast paths vs immutable raw batch data lakes.

concepts.title: Count-min sketch
concepts.summary: Sublinear space frequency estimation using multi-hash 2D arrays to bound overcounting error.

concepts.title: Top-k heavy hitters

concepts.title: Reservoir sampling

concepts.title: t-digest quantile sketch

concepts.title: Streaming percentile analytics

concepts.title: Design: live reactions at high throughput
concepts.summary: Absorbing millions of live stream emoji reactions/sec using lossy aggregation buffers and WebSocket broadcasts.

theory.overview: High-throughput platforms generate billions of metrics, impressions, and events daily. Calculating exact unique counts or running percentiles on billions of rows exhausts memory. This module covers probabilistic sketches: HyperLogLog for cardinality estimation, Count-Min sketch for frequency tracking, Top-K heavy hitters, Reservoir sampling, and t-digest for tail percentiles.
theory.whyItMatters: A single COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) across 500 million records consumes gigabytes of RAM. HyperLogLog computes the same metric within 1% error using only 1.5 KB of memory.
keyMechanisms: Probabilistic cardinality: HyperLogLog leading zero counting, harmonic mean, and mergeable registers.
Frequency estimation: Count-Min sketch 2D array hashing, minimum bound, and top-k heavy hitter queues.
Quantiles & Percentiles: t-digest centroid clustering for precise p99/p99.9 latency monitoring on streaming data.
Stream sampling: Reservoir sampling maintaining unbiased representative samples over infinite streams.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: System design is the end-to-end discipline of architecting large-scale, distributed software platforms from ambiguous product requirements through failure-resilient production deployment. It encompasses calculating capacity bottlenecks, decomposing services, designing storage engines and data models, orchestrating asynchronous streams, and ensuring high availability, fault isolation, and deterministic disaster recovery under extreme traffic.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Modern software systems operate at planetary scale, handling millions of requests per second and petabytes of mutating data across heterogeneous cloud environments. Without rigorous system design principles, architectures suffer from cascading outages, data corruption during split-brain events, runaway cloud infrastructure costs, and insurmountable latency bottlenecks. Mastering system design empowers engineers to transform vague product ambitions into deterministic, cost-efficient, and mathematically sound distributed platforms.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: System design is not the memorization of architecture diagrams; it is the deliberate, rigorous evaluation of trade-offs, physical hardware bounds, and failure modes under stress. Always clarify constraints, calculate back-of-the-envelope bounds, design for failure isolation, and optimize for operational simplicity.
coreArchitectureRules: Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Bounds: Always ground architectural decisions in first-principles calculations: QPS, peak ingress/egress bandwidth, storage growth over 5 years, and cache memory working sets.

CAP & PACELC Trade-Off Theorem: In network partitions (P), trade Consistency (C) for Availability (A). In normal conditions (E), trade Latency (L) for Consistency (C). There is no free lunch in distributed consensus.
Decouple Hot Write Paths from Cold Storage: Separate synchronous, low-latency ingestion queues from heavyweight asynchronous persistence, indexing, and fanout pipelines.

Single Point of Failure (SPOF) Elimination: Every tier—gateways, app servers, caches, message brokers, and databases—must be horizontally partitioned and replicated across availability zones with automatic health checking and failover.
Idempotent Mutations & Safe Retries: Across asynchronous and partitioned networks, network retries and duplicate deliveries are inevitable. Every mutating operation must be keyed idempotently.

Cost-Aware Simplicity: The best infrastructure component is often the one you don't build. Prefer managed, boring technology and vertical headroom until traffic and latency demand distributed horizontal partitioning.

failureModes.name: Cascading Retry Storm (Thundering Herd)
failureModes.description: A momentary database latency spike causes edge API timeouts. Aggressive client retry loops redouble inbound traffic on an already saturated database, pushing latencies to infinity and causing a total site outage.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce exponential backoff with full jitter, circuit breakers on downstream dependencies, and token bucket rate limiters at the edge gateway.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Queue Lag & Worker Exhaustion
failureModes.description: A sudden burst of asynchronous events fills message queues beyond consumer throughput. Worker nodes experience memory exhaustion (OOM), restart repeatedly, and queue processing comes to a complete standstill.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement upstream queue backpressure, partition-based worker horizontal auto-scaling, dead-letter queues (DLQs) for unprocessable poisons, and priority load shedding.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Inconsistency Across Stores
failureModes.description: An application writes to a relational database and attempts to update a Redis cache and Elasticsearch search index in the same request. A partial network failure leaves the cache and search index permanently out of sync with the primary database.
failureModes.mitigation: Adopt the Transactional Outbox pattern or Change Data Capture (CDC) with Debezium to stream committed database write-ahead logs asynchronously into downstream caches and indices.

failureModes.name: Storage Engine Compaction Stall & Write Amplification
failureModes.description: Under high write throughput, Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM) engines fall behind on background SSTable compaction. The storage engine freezes incoming write threads to prevent uncompacted disk exhaustion.
failureModes.mitigation: Tune write buffer sizes, switch from size-tiered to leveled compaction, allocate dedicated NVMe I/O bandwidth for background compaction threads, and buffer bursts with message queues.

failureModes.name: Hot Key & Celebrity Fanout Partition Skew
failureModes.description: In partitioned databases or social feeds, a single celebrity account with 50 million followers triggers millions of simultaneous writes or cache lookups on a single partition key, crashing that individual node.
failureModes.mitigation: Use hybrid fanout: fanout-on-write for standard users, and fanout-on-read with read-side caching for high-follower celebrity accounts. Add random salt prefixes to hot partition keys.

whenToUse: Workloads exceeding 10,000 requests/sec or multi-terabyte datasets requiring horizontal partitioning across nodes.
Platforms requiring 99.99%+ availability SLAs with multi-availability-zone or multi-region automated failover.
Complex domains requiring bounded contexts, decoupled async event pipelines, or distinct read/write scalability profiles.
Systems processing high-velocity real-time event streams, financial ledgers, or high-concurrency bidding/booking engines.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage proof-of-concepts, MVPs, or internal tools where product-market fit is unproven and rapid pivots are paramount.
Applications whose total dataset fits in memory on a single modern server (e.g. 128GB RAM) and QPS is under 500.
Teams lacking automated CI/CD, telemetry, distributed tracing, and dedicated on-call incident response.
Simple transactional CRUD workloads that can be reliably hosted on a single managed PostgreSQL or MySQL instance with read replicas.

tradeOffs.pro: Vertical scaling requires zero distributed consensus, simplifies transactional ACID semantics, and has no cross-node network latency.
tradeOffs.con: Has hard physical limits on CPU/RAM/IOPS and creates a single point of failure with high hardware cost per unit of throughput.

tradeOffs.pro: Cache-aside caches only active working sets, is resilient to cache crashes, and avoids unnecessary cache writes.
tradeOffs.con: Suffers from initial cache miss latency penalties and potential stale read race conditions without proper TTL jitter.

tradeOffs.factor: Push Fanout vs Pull-on-Demand (Hybrid Feed Architecture)
tradeOffs.pro: Push fanout (fanout-on-write) makes feed reads blazing fast O(1) operations by precomputing timelines in Redis.
tradeOffs.con: Wastes storage and CPU on inactive users and creates enormous write latency spikes when celebrity accounts publish.

tradeOffs.factor: Synchronous RPC (gRPC/REST) vs Asynchronous Event Streaming
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous RPC provides immediate caller feedback, simplifies call graph reasoning, and requires no intermediate broker infrastructure.
tradeOffs.con: Couples services tightly in time and availability, allowing a single slow dependency to exhaust thread pools and trigger cascading outages.

tradeOffs.factor: Exact Counting vs Probabilistic Sketching (HyperLogLog & Count-Min)
tradeOffs.pro: Probabilistic sketches compute cardinality and heavy hitters in sub-millisecond time with constant, predictable memory (e.g. 1.5 KB for HyperLogLog).
tradeOffs.con: Sacrifices absolute precision with a standard error bound (~1%), making sketches unsuitable for financial billing or strict auditing.

productionScenarios.title: 10M DAU URL Shortener with Distributed Snowflake IDs
productionScenarios.scenario: A global marketing platform needed to generate 1,000 short URLs per second and resolve 50,000 redirects/sec with global p99 latency under 20ms while preventing sequential ID enumeration.
productionScenarios.outcome: Implemented a dual-path architecture: 64-bit Snowflake ID generator with Base62 encoding on the write path, and multi-tier edge CDN plus Redis cache-aside on the read path with 302 temporary redirects, achieving 8ms p99 latency and 99.995% availability.

productionScenarios.title: Multi-Channel Notification Gateway with Celebrity Fanout Partitioning
productionScenarios.scenario: An e-commerce mobile app experienced 45-minute notification delays when flash sale announcements saturated downstream push notification worker pools.
productionScenarios.outcome: Architected a tiered ingestion pipeline with Kafka topic partitioning, user preference evaluation in Redis with SETNX deduplication, and isolated worker queues per delivery channel (APNs, FCM, SES) with circuit breakers, reducing flash sale broadcast time to under 90 seconds.

productionScenarios.title: Global Ride-Matching Engine with Geohash/H3 Spatial Indexing
productionScenarios.scenario: A ride-hailing network struggled with database CPU spikes when thousands of active drivers sent GPS location pings every 3 seconds, causing rider search timeouts.
productionScenarios.outcome: Migrated driver hot-path coordinates to Redis GEO backed by 52-bit integer Geohashes and partitioned geographic dispatch regions using Uber H3 hexagonal cells. Dispatch latency dropped from 1.2s to 35ms, cutting server infrastructure costs by 64%.

coreChallenges.title: The Tail at Scale & Latency Amplification
coreChallenges.explanation: Fanout RPC calls across tens or hundreds of backend microservices amplify latency. If a single service has a 1% chance of a 1-second spike, a query fanning out to 100 backend services has a 63% chance of experiencing that 1-second tail latency.

coreChallenges.title: Dual-Write Consistency & Distributed Transactions
coreChallenges.explanation: Updating multiple heterogeneous storage systems (e.g. PostgreSQL, Redis, Elasticsearch) without distributed two-phase commit locks inevitably leads to state divergence. Architectures must use the Transactional Outbox pattern and idempotency tokens.

coreChallenges.title: Clock Drift & Distributed Event Ordering
coreChallenges.explanation: Physical quartz clocks on physical servers drift unpredictably. Relying on wall-clock timestamps for distributed event ordering or leader leases leads to silent data corruption; systems must utilize Lamport logical clocks, Vector clocks, or hybrid logical clocks.

coreChallenges.title: Stateful Failover & Compaction Bottlenecks
coreChallenges.explanation: Managing primary database failover without data loss (RPO=0) requires synchronous replication, which increases write latency. Under sustained high write throughput, storage engines face compaction write amplification and disk I/O stalls.

domainDeepDive.architecturalMindset: Staff and Principal system architects do not design the 'perfect' theoretical architecture. They evaluate physical hardware constraints, identify the single most volatile bottleneck, isolate fault domains, and explicitly choose which metric (consistency, latency, or dollar cost) to sacrifice for business survival.
